artifacts.clinical_relevance: It gives clinicians a time-ordered plan while preserving the need to weigh neonatal risks when early-term delivery is preferred.

document_sections.heading: ABSTRACT
document_sections.content: Stillbirth affects 1 in 160 deliveries in the United States. Frequently associated factors in developed countries include non-Hispanic black race, nulliparity, older maternal age, obesity, preexisting diabetes, chronic hypertension, smoking, alcohol use, assisted reproductive technology, multiple gestation, male fetal sex, unmarried status, and obstetric history. Some factors, such as smoking, can be changed, but many cannot. Inconsistent evaluation and classification practices and declining autopsy rates complicate investigation of causes; even extensive assessment may leave the cause undetermined. Evaluation should encompass fetal autopsy, gross and histologic assessment of the placenta, cord, and membranes, and genetic assessment. Gestational age at death, prior obstetric history, and maternal preferences guide delivery method and timing. Clinicians should balance each option’s risks and benefits against institutional expertise. Care should include emotional support and understandable communication of results; referral for grief or depression support may be appropriate.

document_sections.heading: Purpose
document_sections.content: Stillbirth occurs in 1 in 160 U.S. deliveries, with approximately 23,600 cases at 20 weeks or greater of gestation reported each year. This document examines definitions, management, evaluation, and prevention strategies.

document_sections.heading: Background
document_sections.content: The following sections address how stillbirth is defined and measured, its associated risk factors, and potential causes.

document_sections.heading: Definition
document_sections.content: The U.S. National Center for Health Statistics defines fetal death by delivery without evidence of life: breathing, heartbeat, umbilical cord pulsation, or definite voluntary muscle movement. State reporting thresholds for weight and gestational age differ. Suggested reporting covers deaths at 20 weeks or greater when gestational age is known, or fetal weight greater than or equal to 350 grams when it is unknown; 350 grams corresponds to the 50th percentile at 20 weeks. U.S. vital statistics use a stated or presumed gestational duration of 20 weeks or more for comparisons across years and states. Pregnancy terminations for life-limiting fetal anomalies and labor induction for previable premature rupture of membranes are classified as terminations rather than stillbirths. Because parent groups prefer it and recent research uses it, this document uses the term stillbirth.

document_sections.heading: Frequency of Occurrence
document_sections.content: In the United States, the reported stillbirth rate was 5.96 per 1,000 live births in 2013, versus 6.61 in 2006 and 6.05 per 1,000 births in 2012. Early stillbirth at 20–27 weeks changed little during 2006–2012; its rate fell from 3.11 to 3.01 per 1,000 births between 2012 and 2013. Late stillbirth at 28 weeks or greater has been comparatively stable since 2006: rates of 2.96 and 2.97 per 1,000 births in 2012 and 2013 did not differ significantly. The preferred denominator remains under discussion. The commonly used birth-based measure counts stillbirths per 1,000 live births and stillbirths. An alternative uses pregnancies still ongoing at each gestational age: stillbirths during a single gestational week per 1,000 live births and stillbirths at that week or later. This prospective measure may help estimate an individual pregnancy’s risk and compare expectant management with intervention.

document_sections.heading: Risk Factors
document_sections.content: In developed countries, commonly associated factors are non-Hispanic black race, nulliparity, advanced maternal age, obesity, preexisting diabetes, chronic hypertension, tobacco and alcohol use, assisted reproductive technology, multiple gestation, male fetal sex, unmarried status, and previous obstetric outcomes. Smoking is potentially modifiable; many other factors are not.

document_sections.heading: Social Demographic Factors Affecting Stillbirth
document_sections.content: Among non-Hispanic black women, the stillbirth rate exceeds twice that of other racial groups, at 10.53 deaths per 1,000 livebirths and stillbirths. U.S. rates reported for other groups were 4.88 for non-Hispanic white women, 5.22 for Hispanic women, 6.22 for American Indian or Alaska Native women, and 4.68 for Asian or Pacific Islanders. The disparity has multiple possible causes that remain under investigation. Higher rates persist among non-Hispanic black women receiving adequate prenatal care and have been attributed to greater frequencies of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, placental abruption, and premature rupture of membranes. Compared with white women, educational attainment does not appear protective for Hispanic or non-Hispanic black women; the largest white–non-Hispanic black disparities occur at 20–27 weeks regardless of education. Implicit and explicit bias and racism contribute to many perinatal health disparities, but the contributions of biologic factors, modifiable factors, differences in care, environmental stressors, bias, and racism to this particular risk require further characterization.

document_sections.heading: Multiple Gestations
document_sections.content: Twin pregnancies have approximately 2.5 times the singleton stillbirth rate: 14.07 versus 5.65 per 1,000 live births and stillbirths. Risk rises with advancing gestation in all twin pregnancies and is significantly higher with monochorionic than dichorionic twins. The reported rate for triplets and higher-order multiples is 30.53 per 1,000 live births and stillbirths. Contributors include multiple-gestation-specific complications, such as twin–twin transfusion syndrome, and increased risks of aneuploidy, congenital anomalies, and growth restriction.

document_sections.heading: Past Obstetric History
document_sections.content: A previous stillbirth raises the risk in a later pregnancy compared with no such history; the pooled odds ratio was 4.83; 95% CI, 3.77–6.18, and remained significant after adjustment. Previous preterm delivery, growth restriction, or preeclampsia also increases subsequent risk. This association is strongest for stillbirths with an identified cause, although adverse obstetric history remains associated with a 1.7-fold to 2-fold increase in unexplained stillbirth. In one study, a prior SGA birth increased later stillbirth risk most when birth occurred at less than 32 weeks (OR, 8.0; 95% CI, 4.7–13.7). Evidence on prior cesarean delivery is conflicting. Two large United Kingdom studies associated it with subsequent explained and unexplained stillbirth, reporting adjusted hazard ratios of 2.08 (95% CI, 1.00–4.31) and 1.75 (95% CI, 1.30–2.37), respectively, for subsequent stillbirth from all causes. A Danish analysis found small, statistically nonsignificant increases for both categories. Three large U.S. observational studies and one Canadian study found no association. In the largest, term unexplained stillbirth rates were 0.8 versus 0.7 per 1,000 births with versus without previous cesarean delivery (relative risk [RR] 0.90; 95% CI, 0.76–1.06). Nulliparous women and women with greater than three previous pregnancies have higher rates than women with one or two previous births.

document_sections.heading: Male sex
document_sections.content: Male fetal sex is an observed risk factor. A review covering more than 30 million births across high- and low-income countries reported crude mean stillbirth rates per 1,000 total births of 6.23 for males and 5.74 for females. Its pooled RR was 1.10 (95% CI, 1.07–1.13), corresponding to approximately a 10% higher risk for males. The reason for the difference remains unknown.

document_sections.heading: Younger and Older Maternal Age
document_sections.content: Maternal ages less than 15 years and greater than 35 years independently increase stillbirth risk. Age greater than or equal to 35 years is associated with increased risk in both nulliparous and multiparous women. Lethal congenital and chromosomal anomalies account for a substantial share of perinatal deaths in older women; population-based chromosomal screening has contributed to lower rates of explained stillbirth or neonatal death due to chromosomal abnormalities. Large observational studies identify advanced age as an independent risk factor after adjustment for hypertension, diabetes, placenta previa, and multiple gestation. Increasing age and first birth appear to interact. One study estimated stillbirth risk after 37 weeks at 1 in 116 for a 40-year-old nulliparous woman versus 1 in 304 for a multiparous woman of the same age. For mothers younger than 15 years, the rate was 15.88 per 1,000 live births, nearly three times the 5.34 per 1,000 rate at ages 25–29 years. Rates were 7.03 per 1,000 at ages 15–17 years and 6.52 per 1,000 live births at ages 18–19 years, respectively 32% and 22% above the lowest-risk age group. Several studies observed this elevation at both age extremes, including a population cohort of 37,504,230 births.

document_sections.heading: Comorbid Medical Conditions
document_sections.content: The accompanying table estimates stillbirth rates for maternal and fetal conditions. Hypertension and diabetes are common pregnancy comorbidities. Population studies report an almost twofold to fivefold increase in stillbirth risk with pregestational or gestational diabetes. The combined effect of pregestational diabetes and obesity appears stronger than either effect alone. Strict preconception glycemic control targeting HgbA1C less than 7%, followed by maternal euglycemia in pregnancy, may lower risk. Reported perinatal mortality with chronic hypertension is 2–4 times that in the general population; its association with stillbirth or neonatal death appears independent of superimposed preeclampsia or fetal growth restriction. The blood-pressure threshold for treatment in pregnancy remains debated, and whether strict control prevents stillbirth is unknown. Concurrent chronic hypertension and pregestational diabetes appear to confer still greater risk. Systemic lupus erythematosus, renal disease, uncontrolled thyroid disease, and cholestasis of pregnancy have also been associated with stillbirth. The document directs readers to ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 145 for antenatal surveillance guidance based on anticipated risk.

document_sections.heading: Acquired and Inherited Thrombophilias
document_sections.content: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is an acquired thrombophilia associated with stillbirth; diagnosis requires both clinical and laboratory criteria, and prior stillbirth is a clinical criterion. Women with stillbirth are therefore typically assessed for APS. Inherited thrombophilias have not been associated with stillbirth, and testing for them within the stillbirth evaluation is not recommended (1C Strong recommendation, low-quality evidence).

document_sections.heading: Obesity and Gestational Weight Gain
document_sections.content: Obesity is defined by prepregnancy BMI of 30 or greater, with BMI calculated from weight in kilograms divided by squared height in meters. It is described as the fastest-growing U.S. health problem and is associated in pregnancy with early fetal loss and stillbirth. In a study spanning five highincome countries, maternal overweight and obesity (BMI greater than 25) was the most frequent modifiable stillbirth risk factor. A meta-analysis of 38 studies encompassing 16,274 stillbirths associated even modest BMI increases with greater risk: at BMI values of 20, 25, and 30, absolute risks per 1,000 pregnancies were 4.0 (reference standard), 4.8 (95% CI, 46– 51), and 5.9 (95% CI, 55–63), respectively. Excessive gestational weight gain was associated with greater risk among obese and morbidly obese women. Some evidence suggests risk associated with obesity rises later in gestation; one study reported a stillbirth hazard ratio rising from 2.1 at 28–36 weeks to 4.6 at 40 weeks. The association is probably multifactorial. Obesity is associated with a fivefold greater risk of stillbirth attributed to placental dysfunction and remains an independent risk factor after accounting for smoking, gestational diabetes, and preeclampsia. The BMI that minimizes risk is unknown.

document_sections.heading: Substance Use
document_sections.content: Maternal cocaine, methamphetamine, other illicit drug use, and tobacco smoking substantially contribute to placental abruption and stillbirth. In a secondary case–control analysis, illicit drug detection in umbilical cord homogenate was associated with stillbirth (OR, 1.94; 95% CI, 1.16–3.27). Smoking is especially common as a risk factor in high-income countries. A large systematic review associated smoking during pregnancy with a significant 47% increase in stillbirth odds (OR, 1.47; 95% CI, 1.37–1.57, P,.0001). Studies of exposure timing and amount support a causal relationship. Secondhand exposure also increases risk relative to never smokers with little or no such exposure, with risks comparable to those of some active smokers. First-trimester smoking was associated with increased risk (adjusted hazard ratio, 2.4; 95% CI, 1.2–4.9). The smoking association shows a dose response: one to nine cigarettes daily was associated with 9% higher odds than not smoking (OR, 1.09, 95% CI, 1.09– 1.24, P5.55, six studies), while 10 or more daily was associated with 52% higher odds (OR, 1.52; 95% CI, 1.30–1.78, P,.0001, seven studies). Stopping between pregnancies was protective: women who smoked only in their first pregnancy had no increased recurrent risk relative to those who smoked in neither (OR, 1.02; 95% CI, 0.79–1.30); risk among women who smoked in both pregnancies was 1.35 (95% CI, 1.15–1.58).

document_sections.heading: Assisted Reproductive Technology
document_sections.content: Pregnancies following in vitro fertilization (IVF) appear to carry a twofold to threefold increase in stillbirth risk after accounting for age, parity, and multifetal gestation. A California study covering 2009–2011 reported an elevated rate of 5.5 per 1,000. Whether procedures or unmeasured factors related to infertility explain the association is uncertain. A study found that couples waiting 1 year or more to conceive and women conceiving with nonIVF assisted reproductive technology had risk similar to fertile couples and lower than those conceiving with IVF or intracytoplasmic sperm injection; this suggests a possible procedural rather than underlying-infertility contribution.

document_sections.heading: Late-Term and Postterm Pregnancies
document_sections.content: A Cochrane review of 30 RCTs involving 12,479 women associated labor induction, compared with expectant management at term or postterm, with lower risks of perinatal death and cesarean delivery. On the basis of these and observational findings, induction for late-term or postterm pregnancy is recommended after 42 0/7 weeks and may be considered at or after 41 weeks 0/7 days. Estimated stillbirth risk after 41 weeks varies by race and ethnicity from 14–40 per 1,000 live births. In California data from 1997–2006, mortality risks under expectant management and delivery were equivalent at 38 weeks; at later ages, expectant management carried greater mortality, with 17.6 per 10,000 versus 10.8 per 10,000 ongoing pregnancies at 42 weeks. Against the cohort’s 37-week stillbirth reference rate, RR was 2.9 (95% CI, 2.6–3.2) at 41 weeks and 5.1 (95% CI, 4.4–6.0) at 42 weeks.

document_sections.heading: Potential Causes of Stillbirth
document_sections.content: Nonuniform protocols for evaluation and classification and falling autopsy rates obstruct study of specific causes. Certificates are often completed before the full postnatal investigation, and revised certificates are rarely submitted when later results emerge. Establishing a definite cause for an individual death can be difficult; a substantial proportion remains unexplained after thorough investigation.

document_sections.heading: Fetal Growth Restriction
document_sections.content: Growth restriction substantially increases stillbirth risk, especially when fetal weight is less than the 2.5th percentile. Cumulative risk is approximately 1.5% below the 10th percentile and 2.5% below the 5th percentile for gestational age. In an analysis of U.S. births, estimated growth below the 3rd percentile carried the highest rate, 58.0 per 10,000 at risk, compared with 43.9 per 10,000 at risk below the 5th percentile and 26.3 per 10,000 at risk below the 10th percentile. Associated fetal aneuploidies and infection and maternal smoking, hypertension, autoimmune disease, obesity, and diabetes also modify risk.

document_sections.heading: Placental Abruption
document_sections.content: Abruption is identified as the cause in 5–10% of stillbirths. Maternal cocaine and other illicit drugs and tobacco contribute substantially to both abruption and stillbirth. Abruption is more likely to cause death when the fetus is preterm or a greater placental area is involved. Abruption rates appear to be increasing. Hemodynamically important fetomaternal hemorrhage without abruption rarely causes stillbirth and occurs mainly in unusual settings such as chorioangioma or choriocarcinoma.

document_sections.heading: Chromosomal and Genetic Abnormalities
document_sections.content: An abnormal karyotype is found in approximately 6–13% of stillbirths. Its frequency exceeds 20% with fetal anatomical abnormalities or growth restriction; one large series found chromosomal anomalies in 4.6% of normally formed fetuses. Among abnormal stillbirth karyotypes, trisomy 21 accounted for 31%, monosomy X for 22%, trisomy 18 for 22%, and trisomy 13 for 8%. Karyotyping underestimates genetic contributions because culture fails in up to 50% of attempts. Chorionic villi sampling or amniocentesis before delivery can improve culture yield: a Netherlands study reported 85% with invasive testing versus 28% with postbirth fetal tissue. If invasive testing is declined, placental tissue, a cord segment, or internal fetal tissue can be submitted for genetic analysis (1B Strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). Microarray detects aneuploidy and copy number variants too small for karyotyping. Compared with karyotyping, its reported diagnosis of a genetic cause increased to 41.9% across all stillbirths, 34.5% in antepartum stillbirths, and 53.8% when anomalies were present. Its advantage includes use of nonviable tissue and particular value with congenital anomalies or unavailable karyotypes; incorporation into evaluation improves successful testing and anomaly detection (1A Strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). Microarrray is preferred, although cost and logistics may leave karyotyping as the accessible option. Whole exome sequencing and whole genome sequencing may become relevant but are not presently standard. Confined placental mosaicism has been associated with increased risk but is not standard testing. Spontaneous autosomal dominant mutations, such as those causing skeletal dysplasias, and inherited parental mutations causing long QT syndrome may contribute. Routine single-gene and microdeletion assessment is currently limited because no single defect is likely to explain a substantial share. Testing for particular genetic abnormalities should follow the clinical history and observed fetal abnormalities (1C Strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). Approximately 20% of stillborn fetuses show dysmorphic or skeletal findings, and 15–20% have a major malformation.

document_sections.heading: Infection
document_sections.content: In developed countries, infection is associated with approximately 10–20% of stillbirths; its share is larger in developing countries. In developed countries it accounts for a greater proportion of preterm than term stillbirths. Possible pathways are direct fetal infection, placental dysfunction, severe maternal illness, and triggering of spontaneous preterm birth. Infection may ascend, as with group B streptococcus or Escherichia coli, or spread hematogenously, as with Listeria monocytogenes or syphilis. Associated viruses include cytomegalovirus, parvovirus, and Zika. Serologic testing for toxoplasmosis, rubella, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex virus is not recommended because benefit has not been established.

document_sections.heading: Umbilical Cord Events
document_sections.content: Cord abnormalities account for approximately 10% of stillbirths, but causal attribution requires caution. In a cohort–control study of almost 14,000 deliveries, single nuchal cords occurred in 23.6% and multiple nuchal cords in 3.7%; neither was associated with increased stillbirth risk. The Stillbirth Collaborative Research Network required findings such as vasa previa, cord entrapment, occlusion with fetal hypoxia, prolapse, or stricture with thrombi to attribute death to the cord. A nuchal cord by itself was insufficient, and other causes should be excluded.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Considerations and Management
document_sections.content: This part addresses the components of evaluation, delivery after confirmed death, bereavement care, and care in later pregnancies.

document_sections.heading: ► What are the essential components of a stillbirth evaluation?
document_sections.content: The evaluation should include fetal autopsy, gross and histologic examination of the placenta, umbilical cord, and membranes, and genetic assessment (1A Strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). The document also presents evaluation diagrams and an assessment of test utility across clinical circumstances.

document_sections.heading: Examination of the Placenta
document_sections.content: Examination of the placenta, cord, and membranes by a pathologist trained in gross and microscopic assessment is the most useful single component of stillbirth evaluation and is essential (1A Strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). Gross findings can identify abruption, cord thrombosis, velamentous insertion, or vasa previa. Placental assessment can inform investigation of infection, genetic abnormalities, and anemia. For multifetal gestations, vascular and membrane assessment is especially informative; chorionicity and vascular anastomoses should be determined. Cord knots or entanglement warrant documentation but cautious interpretation: entanglement occurs in approximately 25% of normal pregnancies, and most true knots are identified after live birth. Before attributing death to a cord accident, seek supporting evidence of occlusion and hypoxia on postmortem and placental or cord histology. Minimal histologic findings include vascular ectasia and thrombosis in the cord, chorionic plate, and stem villi; a regional pattern of avascular villi or stromal karyorrhexis is additionally suggested for a probable diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: Examination of the Stillborn Fetus
document_sections.content: Examine the fetus promptly for dysmorphic findings and measure weight, length, and head circumference (1C Strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). Before 23 weeks, foot length may be especially helpful for estimating gestational age. Whole-body photographs without clothing, frontal and profile facial images, extremity and palm images, and close-ups of anomalies support later specialist review, particularly where a geneticist is unavailable. Offer fetal autopsy because it is among the most informative tests for cause of death (1A Strong recommendation, high-quality evidence); its yield is greater with dysmorphism, discordant growth measurements, anomalies, hydrops, or growth restriction. When families decline complete autopsy, options include partial autopsy, trained-pathologist gross examination, ultrasonography, and especially magnetic resonance imaging. Parents should have an opportunity to hold their baby and observe cultural or religious practices before autopsy. Wholebody X-ray in anterior–posterior and lateral views can reveal or clarify skeletal abnormalities. A full autopsy should follow published perinatal protocols, including measurements such as foot length and body weight to estimate gestational age, an estimate of time from death to delivery, investigation of developmental and intrinsic abnormalities, and evaluation for infection. Preferably, an experienced perinatal pathologist performs it and a clinician experienced in genetics and dysmorphology examines the fetus. The obstetric and relevant medical history and requests for additional tissue collection should be conveyed to pathology.

document_sections.heading: Fetal Laboratory Studies
document_sections.content: After appropriate parental permission, genetic analysis should be performed for every stillbirth because of its diagnostic yield (1A Strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). Karyotype and microarray yield more information with dysmorphism, inconsistent growth measures, anomalies, hydrops, or growth restriction. Comparative genomic hybridization or single nucleotide probe and copy number probe microarrays provide almost the same information as karyotype while detecting smaller chromosomal abnormalities; single nucleotide probe arrays also identify uniparental disomy and consanguinity. Fetal karyotyping matters if a parent carries a balanced rearrangement, such as translocation or inversion, or has mosaicism. Suitable samples include amniotic fluid, a placental block beneath cord insertion incorporating the chorionic plate, cord tissue, and internal fetal tissue able to grow at low oxygen tension, such as costochondral or patellar tissue. Fetal skin is suboptimal. Amniocentesis for karyotyping has the greatest yield, particularly if delivery is not imminent. Laboratory requests should provide relevant history and examination findings for cytogenetic interpretation (Best practice). Because costs can affect parental decisions, anticipated genetic-testing costs should be communicated when possible.

document_sections.heading: Maternal Evaluation
document_sections.content: Obtain a detailed maternal history of conditions and symptoms associated with stillbirth (Best practice). Include medical and obstetric history, exposures such as drugs and viral infections, and a three-generation family pedigree recording stillbirths. Document and investigate pertinent maternal or paternal family findings. Recurrent losses and relatives born alive with developmental delay or structural anomalies can suggest single-gene disease; consanguinity raises concern for severe autosomal recessive disorders. Ask about arrhythmia and sudden death, including sudden infant death syndrome, because prolonged QT syndrome may be associated with stillbirth. Obtain original clinical records when feasible and record gestational dating by last menstrual period, maternal examinations, laboratory findings, and ultrasonography for comparison with fetal findings. Also consider infection, abruption, and cord abnormalities. Because Kleihaur-Betke findings can rise falsely after delivery, assess significant fetomaternal hemorrhage with Kleihaur-Betke or flow cytometry as soon as possible after diagnosis. APS testing is recommended for many stillbirths, particularly alongside growth restriction, severe preeclampsia, or other evidence of placental insufficiency. Testing includes lupus anticoagulant and immunoglobulin G and immunoglobulin M for anticardiolipin and b2-glycoprotein antibodies. A titer greater than 40 immunoglobulin M phospholipid or immunoglobulin G phospholipid, or greater than 99th percentile, is considered positive but requires confirmation after 12 weeks. Elevated anticardiolipin and anti-b2-glycoprotein-I antibodies are associated with threefold to fivefold higher stillbirth odds, supporting testing in otherwise unexplained cases. Inherited thrombophilia testing is not recommended. In a Stillbirth Collaborative Research Network study of 512 fully evaluated stillbirths, components judged useful for establishing cause were placental pathology, 64.6% (95% CI, 57.9–72.0); fetal autopsy, 42.4% (95% CI, 36.9–48.4); karyotype or microarray, 11.9% (95% CI, 9.1–15.3); antiphospholipid antibodies, 11.1% (95% CI, 8.4– 14.4); fetal–maternal hemorrhage testing, 6.4% (95% CI, 4.4– 9.1); glucose screening, 1.6% (95% CI, 0.7–3.1); parvovirus testing, 0.4% (95% CI, 0.0–1.4); and syphilis testing, 0.2% (95% CI, 0.0–1.1). Utility differed by presentation, favoring an individualized approach. Placental pathology and autopsy were most useful, followed by genetics and antiphospholipid antibody testing; clinical circumstances and postmortem and histologic findings guide further investigation.

document_sections.heading: ► What are the options for management of the current pregnancy after confirmation of a diagnosis of stillbirth?
document_sections.content: Delivery planning should account for gestational age at death, previous obstetric procedures, patient preferences, and the comparative risks and benefits of available methods.

document_sections.heading: Methods of Delivery
document_sections.content: Delivery method and timing depend on gestational age, obstetric history such as previous hysterotomy, and maternal preference. Most patients prefer prompt delivery, but timing is generally not critical because coagulopathy from prolonged fetal retention is uncommon. Usual options are dilation and evacuation or induction. In the second trimester, dilation and evacuation can be offered when an experienced practitioner is available, with counseling that it may reduce the ability to identify gross fetal abnormalities at autopsy and often prevents seeing or holding the fetus afterward. Early second-trimester induction frequently requires subsequent dilation and curettage to remove the placenta. For fetal death at 14 weeks to 24 weeks, induction has been associated with greater maternal morbidity, chiefly infection requiring intravenous antibiotics, than surgical evacuation. At 13 weeks to 24 weeks, induction was also less effective and had more complications than dilation and evacuation (adjusted risk ratio, 8.5; 95% CI, 3.7– 19.8). Clinicians should weigh options in context, consider institutional expertise, and use shared decision-making (Best practice). Before 28 weeks, vaginal misoprostol appears the most efficient induction method regardless of Bishop score; high-dose oxytocin is also acceptable. A meta-analysis of 14 randomized controlled trials found both oral and vaginal misoprostol regimens 100% effective at uterine evacuation within 48 hours for second- and third-trimester stillbirth, although differing doses and schedules hinder comparison. On limited evidence, typical vaginal misoprostol dosing before 28 weeks is 400–600 micrograms every 3–6 hours; less than 400 micrograms is less effective. After 28 weeks, use usual obstetric induction protocols. High-quality evidence supports mifepristone plus misoprostol rather than misoprostol alone for loss before 20 weeks; evidence for adding mifepristone at 24–28 weeks is more limited. Oral mifepristone, either 200 or 600 mg, can precede misoprostol and shorten time to delivery without apparently improving overall induction success; when available, give it 24–48 hours before misoprostol. A previous hysterotomy does not eliminate either induction or dilation and evacuation as an option. In a population case–control study of 611 stillbirths, 91% (41 of 45) with a prior cesarean delivered vaginally following induction, with two uterine ruptures. Induction is generally preferred over cesarean for fetal death, but the scar changes management. Studies have assessed misoprostol 400 micrograms every 6 hours with a prior uterine scar at 24 to 28 weeks; randomized-trial evidence supports vaginal misoprostol before 24 weeks for nonviable pregnancy. More study is needed on effectiveness, safety, route, and dose, especially at 24 weeks to 28 weeks, when 200 micrograms per dose may be preferable. After 28 weeks with previous hysterotomy, follow trial-of-labor-after-cesarean protocols instead of giving misoprostol. At that gestation, a transcervical Foley catheter for cervical ripening has been associated with rupture rates comparable to spontaneous labor and may help when the cervix is unfavorable. Limited evidence favors trial of labor with one previous low transverse cesarean. Prior classical or multiple cesareans require individualized planning because data are limited. Generally reserve cesarean for unusual circumstances: it carries potential maternal morbidity without fetal benefit. Repeat cesarean is reasonable when rupture risk is increased, for example after classical hysterotomy or transfundal surgery. Patients at increased rupture risk choosing induction should understand that risk, and clinicians should monitor for rupture throughout labor.

document_sections.heading: ► What support services and clinical counseling should be offered to the patient with a stillbirth?
document_sections.content: Provide emotional support and explain results clearly. Tailor bereavement care to parents’ personal, cultural, and religious needs (Best practice). Elements include effective communication, joint decisions, recognition of parenthood, attention to partners’ and relatives’ grief and individual grieving patterns, discussion of burial and other arrangements, continued emotional and practical assistance, bereavement training for clinicians, and staff access to self-care. Referral to bereavement counseling, peer support, or mental health services may help with grief and depression. Guilt and anger are common and may intensify when a child has an abnormality or a genetic defect; some parents instead find discussion and autopsy results relieving. Test results matter even without an identified diagnosis. Communicate autopsy, placental, laboratory, and cytogenetic findings promptly to involved clinicians and the family (Best practice). If fetal chromosomes could not be cultured or obtained, consultation with genetics or maternal–fetal medicine is advised to consider parental chromosomal testing. Provide test results and a list of excluded diagnoses if patients wish.

document_sections.heading: ► For the patient with a history of an unexplained stillbirth in a previous pregnancy, how should clinical management be altered in subsequent pregnancies?
document_sections.content: Evidence to direct care after unexplained stillbirth is scarce. Women should be encouraged to reduce modifiable risks, for example by optimizing glycemic control with diabetes. A 2018 Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to determine which interventions effectively improve subsequent-pregnancy care after stillbirth.

document_sections.heading: Risk of Stillbirth Recurrence Counseling
document_sections.content: Recurrence estimates remain limited and disputed; uncertainty about the prior cause complicates counseling, and deaths may remain unexplained after complete investigation. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 cohort and three case–control studies reported stillbirth in 2.5% of women with prior stillbirth versus 0.4% with prior live birth (pooled OR, 4.83; 95% CI, 3.77–6.18). The authors could not pool results specifically for prior unexplained deaths. Two included studies reported adjusted subsequent risks after unexplained stillbirth of 3.11 (95% CI, 0.72–13.50) and 1.00 (95% CI, 0.23–4.30). A retrospective analysis reported an adjusted risk of unexplained stillbirth after one previous stillbirth of 4.18 (95% CI, 1.36–12.89). Identified causes may permit more precise recurrence estimates. Recurrence is greater with maternal diabetes or hypertension and recurrent obstetric conditions such as abruption. Patients may remain anxious despite reassurance and need added support.

document_sections.heading: Antepartum Surveillance
document_sections.content: Evidence guiding surveillance after unexplained stillbirth is limited. Relative to women whose first infant was live born, those with a first stillborn infant were 2.5 times (95% CI, 1.4–4.7) more likely to experience another stillbirth. Depending on race and features of the earlier death—including cause, gestational age, and growth restriction—risk may reach a 10-fold increase. Linked maternal cohort data reported 22.7 per 1,000 with prior stillbirth versus 4.7 per 1,000 without. Prior cause also affects whether testing can prevent recurrence, but frequently is unknown. With a cause such as hypertension or diabetes, surveillance should follow management guidance for that condition. After a stillbirth at or after 32 0/7 weeks, once- or twice-weekly surveillance is recommended from 32 0/7 weeks or 1–2 weeks before the gestational age of the earlier death; after loss before 32 0/7 weeks, individualized initiation may be considered (2C Weak recommendation, low-quality evidence). Surveillance can impose costs and harm: delivery following abnormal or equivocal findings occurred in 16.3% at or before 39 weeks and 1% before 36 weeks. One study estimated that testing before 37 weeks produces a 1.5% rate of iatrogenic prematurity from false-positive results. Excess infant mortality associated with late preterm birth is 8.8 per 1,000 live births at 32–33 weeks and 3 per 1,000 at 34–36 weeks, a consideration when surveillance could lead to early delivery.

document_sections.heading: Fetal Kick Counting for Women with History of Unexplained Stillbirth
document_sections.content: Reports of reduced fetal movement are associated in multiple studies with worse perinatal outcomes. Although kick counting is inexpensive, whether it prevents stillbirth is uncertain. One study linked consistent patient information and standardized clinician guidance for reduced movement with lower stillbirth rates. A large randomized study of movement awareness did not show reduced stillbirth and observed more inductions and hospital admissions. Data are insufficient for specific kick-count recommendations. Suggested practice emphasizes awareness of usual movement patterns, taking reports of reduced movements seriously, systematic responses, and shared decisions about safe interventions.

document_sections.heading: Timing of Delivery
document_sections.content: An early-delivery decision to prevent stillbirth must balance possible benefit against increased maternal and neonatal complications; the risk of continuing pregnancy varies with current maternal and fetal conditions. Delivery before 39 weeks increases admission to neonatal special care for respiratory and other morbidity. Anxiety after prior stillbirth may nevertheless justify early-term birth at 37 0/7 weeks to 38 6/7 weeks when the woman understands and accepts neonatal risks. Decisions should incorporate all maternal and fetal factors and compare early-term birth with continuing pregnancy. Amniocentesis to assess fetal lung maturity generally should not determine delivery timing. The accompanying box outlines care across a subsequent pregnancy.

document_sections.content: This table brings together graded recommendations on inherited thrombophilia testing, genetic sampling and analysis, fetal and placental examinations, maternal history, shared delivery decisions, timely communication, bereavement care, and surveillance after previous stillbirth. Its grades include 1A Strong recommendation, high-quality evidence; 1B Strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence; 1C Strong recommendation, low-quality evidence; Best practice; and 2C Weak recommendation, low-quality evidence.

document_sections.heading: Table 3. Elements of a Stillbirth Evaluation
document_sections.content: This table outlines family, maternal, obstetric, and current-pregnancy history; fetal autopsy and alternatives; placental examination; fetal karyotype/microarray; testing at the time of death; and tests for selected circumstances. It notes that fetal autopsy provides important information in approximately 30% of cases, placental examination adds information in 30% of cases, infection is more frequent in preterm than term stillbirth (19% vs. 2% at term), and fetal genetic abnormalities are found in approximately 8% of cases. It discourages routine inherited thrombophilia testing while noting consideration with a personal or family thromboembolic history.

document_sections.heading: Table 4. Principles of Bereavement Care
document_sections.content: The table describes individualized care responsive to family wishes; clear, honest, parent-sensitive language; sufficient information and time for decisions; recognition of parenthood and opportunities to create memories; support for partners and relatives; acceptance of differing grief responses; respectful discussion of burial, cremation, and funeral choices irrespective of gestational age; continuing professional and peer support, including First Candle; clinician bereavement training; and access to staff self-care.

document_sections.heading: Box 1. Management of Subsequent Pregnancy After Stillbirth
document_sections.content: Before pregnancy or at the first prenatal visit, the box calls for detailed medical and obstetric history, review of the previous death and its investigation, recurrence-risk assessment, smoking cessation, prepregnancy weight loss for obese women, genetic counseling where a familial genetic condition exists, diabetes screening, and acquired thrombophilia tests for lupus anticoagulant and IgG and IgM against anticardiolipin and b2-glycoprotein antibodies, alongside support and reassurance. In the first trimester it lists dating ultrasonography; screening with pregnancy-associated plasma protein A, human chorionic gonadotropin, and nuchal translucency, or cell-free fetal DNA testing; and support. The first-trimester screen modifies risk assessment but does not change management. In the second trimester it lists an anatomic ultrasound at 18–20 weeks, genetic screening if not already performed or single marker alpha fetoprotein after first-trimester screening, and support. In the third trimester it lists growth-restriction screening by ultrasound after 28 weeks and antepartum surveillance starting at 32 weeks or 1–2 weeks ahead of the gestational age of the earlier stillbirth, with continued support. It plans delivery at 39 0/7 weeks unless maternal or fetal conditions indicate otherwise. With severe anxiety and a preference for delivery at 37 0/7 weeks to 38 6/7 weeks, the decision must account for increased neonatal complications relative to possible prevention of recurrence.
